# How Shared Travel Demand Can Connect Offshore Wind


Jaa artikkeli:


20.11.2026


Customer stories


Customer Story | Vestas


Getting offshore wind technicians to the right place at the right time isn’t always straightforward. Teams are spread across Europe, while many offshore projects, installation ports and service bases are located far from international airports and established transport connections.


For Vestas, this creates a particular challenge when mobilising technicians to locations such as Eemshaven and Emden. Reaching these areas from Denmark or the UK can involve lengthy journeys, making crew changes more complicated and taking valuable time away from both work and home.


Kees-Jan van Engelenburg, Lead Aviation Operations Manager at Vestas, explains:


“Ideally, you want your on-signing crew to start their shifts as fresh as possible and get the off-signers home as quickly as possible to keep them motivated for the whole project.”


## Making regional travel work


LYGG’s scheduled regional air connections offer a way to address these challenges by connecting business regions that are not served by existing flight networks.


“LYGG offers the potential to connect these regional hubs to reduce overall travel time for technicians. It provides greater flexibility for sites, the potential to reduce hotel costs, fatigue and non-productive travel hours paid by the employer,” says van Engelenburg.


## From one challenge to a shared solution


Offshore wind projects bring together multiple companies, contractors and specialist teams. While they often travel to the same locations, their journeys are frequently organised separately.


On Vestas projects, most technicians work for established subcontractors. This makes cooperation between different companies particularly important when planning efficient crew transportation.


For van Engelenburg, the key is bringing travel demand together and building connections around the industry’s operational needs. He explains:


“In offshore wind, we have fixed crew-change patterns, regardless of the dynamic of the operation. The one who can combine this and customise has the highest chance of success here. You need to understand and meet that demand and the priority of the applicable project, not the other way around.”


As with helicopters, charter flights need combined volume to be cost-effective and sustainable in the long term. Most Vestas technicians work for subcontractors, so cooperation between Vestas, its subcontractors and other partners operating in the same wind farms is what makes regular flights possible. Van Engelenburg adds:


“Cooperation between Vestas, its subcontractors and potentially other partners operating within the same wind farms is what will make this work on a regular basis.”


## Better connectivity through cooperation


As van Engelenburg puts it:


“As an industry, we all have the same logistical challenges, but we all search for our own solutions. Even within one wind farm, we often have different logistical solutions for the same problem.”


By bringing travel demand together, the industry can make better use of transport capacity, improve regional connectivity and reduce unnecessary travel time for specialists.
